title: From Al-Mujadila to Al-Mursalat
intro: 26 days through surahs 58 to 77, from Al-Mujadila to Al-Mursalat, one verse at a time.

posts.display_original: قَدْ سَمِعَ ٱللَّهُ قَوْلَ ٱلَّتِى تُجَٰدِلُكَ فِى زَوْجِهَا وَتَشْتَكِىٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَٱللَّهُ يَسْمَعُ تَحَاوُرَكُمَآ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَمِيعٌۢ بَصِيرٌ
posts.caption: This plan walks through surahs 58 to 77, beginning with Al-Mujadila, "The Woman Who Pleads", a Medinan surah of 22 verses and the only one with the name Allah in every verse. Classical commentators say it opens with Khawlah bint Tha'labah, who brought a complaint about her husband to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and was heard.

Al-Hashr, "The Exile", is a Medinan surah of 24 verses, and its last three verses gather many of the names of Allah. They begin here: the Knower of the unseen and the seen, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, the Beneficent and the Merciful. Many Muslims memorise and recite the three verses together.

Eight names of Allah in a single verse, among them al-Malik (the Sovereign), al-Quddus (the Holy), as-Salam (Peace), al-Mu'min (the Keeper of Faith, or Giver of Safety) and al-Jabbar (the Compeller). The verse ends by declaring Allah far above any partner people ascribe to Him.

The last verse of Al-Hashr names Allah as al-Khaliq, al-Bari' and al-Musawwir, which commentators explain as three stages of creating: planning, bringing into being, and giving form. "The most beautiful names" is al-asma' al-husna, the names Muslims traditionally count as ninety-nine.

Al-Mumtahanah, "The Woman Examined", is a Medinan surah of 13 verses from a time of open hostility between the Muslims of Medina and the Quraysh of Mecca. This verse holds out hope that enemies may yet become loved ones. Commentators note that many Meccans did later embrace Islam.

As-Saff, "The Ranks", is a Medinan surah of 14 verses. These two verses ask a direct question about the gap between words and deeds, and call that gap "most hateful in the sight of Allah". The concern is integrity: saying and doing belong together.

Al-Jumu'ah, "Friday" or "The Congregation", is a Medinan surah of 11 verses, named for the Friday congregational prayer. The verse before calls believers to hurry to that prayer and set aside trade; this one sends them back out to work and earn, with Allah still in mind.

Al-Munafiqun, "The Hypocrites", is a Medinan surah of 11 verses. Its closing verses turn to the believers, urging them to give from what they have been given before death comes. The words of the dying person, asking for just a little more time to give in charity, are among the Quran's most moving.

At-Taghabun, "Mutual Disillusion", has 18 verses and is usually classed as Medinan. Its name refers to the Day of Judgment, when people learn who truly gained and who lost. The early scholar Alqamah is reported to have explained this verse as someone struck by misfortune who knows it comes from Allah and accepts it.

posts.display: And whosoever keepeth his duty to Allah, Allah will appoint a way out for him, and will provide for him from (a quarter) whence he hath no expectation. And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him.
posts.display_original: وَمَن يَتَّقِ ٱللَّهَ يَجْعَل لَّهُۥ مَخْرَجًا وَيَرْزُقْهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَحْتَسِبُ وَمَن يَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ فَهُوَ حَسْبُهُۥٓ
posts.caption: At-Talaq, "Divorce", is a Medinan surah of 12 verses. In the middle of its rules for separation come some of the Quran's most quoted lines on trust. Whoever keeps their duty to Allah (taqwa) is promised a way out and provision from where they never expected, and whoever relies on Him (tawakkul) will find Him enough.

posts.display: And Allah citeth an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh when she said: My Lord! Build for me a home with thee in the Garden, and deliver me from Pharaoh and his work, and deliver me from evil-doing folk.
posts.caption: At-Tahrim, "The Prohibition", is a Medinan surah of 12 verses. It ends by holding up two women as examples for all believers: Pharaoh's wife, known in Islamic tradition as Asiya, and Maryam (Mary). Living in a tyrant's palace, Asiya prayed for a home near Allah and for rescue from Pharaoh.

posts.display: Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and He is Able to do all things.
posts.display_original: تَبَٰرَكَ ٱلَّذِى بِيَدِهِ ٱلْمُلْكُ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
posts.caption: Al-Mulk, "The Sovereignty", is a Meccan surah of 30 verses. Many Muslims recite it every night before sleep, following hadith that praise it as a protector of the one who reads it. It opens with the source of all authority: everything is in Allah's hand.

posts.display: Who hath created life and death that He may try you which of you is best in conduct; and He is the Mighty, the Forgiving.
posts.caption: Life and death are both described as created, and both serve a purpose: to show who is best in conduct. The Arabic, ahsanu 'amala, speaks of the best deeds, not the most. The early scholar Fudayl ibn Iyad explained "best" as most sincere and most correct.

The seven heavens are described as made "in harmony", layer upon layer, without flaw. The reader is invited to look, and look again, for any rift; the next verse says the eye will come back tired, having found none. Pickthall's "Beneficent One" is ar-Rahman.

A simple, everyday sight: birds spreading and folding their wings in flight. The verse says it is ar-Rahman, the Beneficent, who holds them up. Al-Mulk keeps pointing to ordinary things, from the sky to the water we drink, as signs of Allah's care.

Al-Qalam, "The Pen", is a Meccan surah of 52 verses, among the earliest revealed, comforting the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when opponents called him mad. "Nature" translates khuluq, character. A well-known hadith sums up his character in a phrase: it was the Quran.

Al-Haqqah, "The Reality", is a Meccan surah of 52 verses about the Day of Judgment. Receiving one's record in the right hand is the Quran's image of success. This person's joy is also relief: they lived knowing a reckoning would come, and prepared for it.

Al-Ma'arij, "The Ascending Stairways", is a Meccan surah of 44 verses. This is a frank portrait of human nature: anxious, fretful in hardship, tight-fisted in good times. The exception is the worshippers, and the verses that follow describe them: constant in prayer, generous to the poor, true to their word.

posts.display: And I have said: Seek pardon of your Lord. Lo! He was ever Forgiving. He will let loose the sky for you in plenteous rain.
posts.caption: Nuh is a Meccan surah of 28 verses, devoted entirely to the Prophet Nuh (Noah) and his long mission. Here he tells his people that seeking forgiveness (istighfar) brings mercy, even rain. Classical commentators tell of Hasan al-Basri citing these verses to people who came to him complaining of drought and poverty.

posts.display: Say (O Muhammad): It is revealed unto me that a company of the jinn gave ear, and they said: Lo! it is a marvellous Qur'an.
posts.display_original: قُلْ أُوحِىَ إِلَىَّ أَنَّهُ ٱسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌ مِّنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَقَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا سَمِعْنَا قُرْءَانًا عَجَبًا
posts.caption: Al-Jinn is a Meccan surah of 28 verses, told largely in the voice of jinn: unseen beings who, in Islamic belief, have free will like humans. A group of them heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reciting the Quran and were amazed. The surah relays what they said to one another.

posts.display: O thou wrapped up in thy raiment! Keep vigil the night long, save a little - A half thereof, or abate a little thereof Or add (a little) thereto - and chant the Qur'an in measure.
posts.display_original: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمُزَّمِّلُ قُمِ ٱلَّيْلَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا نِّصْفَهُۥٓ أَوِ ٱنقُصْ مِنْهُ قَلِيلًا أَوْ زِدْ عَلَيْهِ وَرَتِّلِ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ تَرْتِيلًا
posts.caption: Al-Muzzammil, "The Enwrapped One", is an early Meccan surah of 20 verses, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ wrapped in his garments. It calls him to pray through much of the night and to recite with tartil, slow and measured. The surah's long final verse later lightens the night vigil.

posts.display_original: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمُدَّثِّرُ قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ وَرَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ وَٱلرُّجْزَ فَٱهْجُرْ
posts.caption: Al-Muddaththir, "The Cloaked One", is a Meccan surah of 56 verses. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari places these verses after a pause in revelation that followed the first verses of Al-Alaq. They mark the call to begin preaching; commentators explain "pollution" as the worship of idols.

Al-Qiyamah, "The Resurrection", is a Meccan surah of 40 verses. It answers those who doubted that scattered bones could live again: Allah is able to restore even the fingers, which commentators take as the fingertips, the finest detail of a person. The surah closes on the same note: is the One who shaped human life not able to bring the dead to life?

posts.display_original: هَلْ أَتَىٰ عَلَى ٱلْإِنسَٰنِ حِينٌ مِّنَ ٱلدَّهْرِ لَمْ يَكُن شَيْـًٔا مَّذْكُورًا
posts.caption: Al-Insan, "Man", also called Ad-Dahr, "Time", has 31 verses. It opens with a question that invites humility: there was a time before each of us existed, when we were nothing worth mentioning. Many Muslims know it from the Friday dawn prayer, where it is often recited with As-Sajdah.

posts.display: And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him, (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you.
posts.caption: A portrait of the righteous: they feed the poor, the orphan and the captive, and seek no thanks. Commentators read "for love of Him" two ways: out of love for Allah, or despite their own love of the food. Either way, the giving is quiet and expects nothing back.

Al-Mursalat, "The Emissaries", is a Meccan surah of 50 verses in which a refrain of warning returns ten times. Early commentators explained the "receptacle" as the earth holding the living on its surface and the dead within it. That closes this journey from Al-Mujadila to Al-Mursalat; thank you for reading along.
